messages:
marcus.cs: FYI escalation from a customer — they're seeing p99 TTFB spikes on streaming endpoints only. Non-streaming (single response) latency looks normal. Customer provided request IDs and a short repro.

julia.support: cc @lee.eng @sam.sre for triage. customer is on hosted tier, region us-west-2, started ~35m ago after a deployment. They see p50 ~150ms but p99 TTFB jumps to ~2.1s specifically for the first chunk. Total time is unchanged when they switch to non-streaming.

lee.eng: can you paste the request id and a minimal curl repro? streaming vs non-streaming example would help.

marcus.cs: pasted their snippet:
```
# streaming (observed slow first chunk)
curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","stream":true,"prompt":"short"}' \
  https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate --no-buffer

# non-streaming (fast)
curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","stream":false,"prompt":"short"}' \
  https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate
```
They included request_id=rid_0ab3c5 and headers dump.

lee.eng: thanks. initial theory: streaming uses small chunk flush timers + continuous batching. If a coalescing timer or proxy buffering delays the first flush, TTFB will jump even if backend generation is fast. Could be nginx/gateway buffering or our fronting CDN.

sam.sre: confirmed we had a canary nginx config tweak rolled out to us-west yesterday that enabled proxy_buffering by default for SSE endpoints (to reduce connection churn). That would exactly cause first-chunk hold-back. Checking deploy logs... @deploy-bot any recent change?

deploy-bot: deploy 2026-03-14T21:10:12Z applied: router/nginx: fallback-proxy-buffering=true (canary to 20% of nodes in us-west-2).

julia.support: that aligns with customer timeline. Can we test toggling buffering off for their tenant or route?

lee.eng: quick reproducible local test — I ran a small server that writes first chunk immediately then sleeps; with proxy_buffering on I see ~1.9s delay before the client gets chunk. With proxy_buffering off it arrives ~40ms. So proxy buffering is likely cause.

taylor.eng: another possibility: HTTP/2 flow control + chunk coalescing at the edge. But nginx proxy_buffering for chunked responses is more likely given the canary. Also check our streaming flush_after_ms default. If we recently increased default from 10ms->50ms for batching, that could add to p99.

sam.sre: checking metrics -> there is a p99 bump for first_chunk_latency in us-west-2 starting at 21:15 UTC. Correlates with canary rollout.

marcus.cs: customer wants a mitigation now — they rely on low TTFB for streaming UX. Any temporary workarounds?

lee.eng: options: 1) disable proxy_buffering for streaming routes (nginx header X-Accel-Buffering: no), 2) adjust canary to exclude streaming traffic / specific tenants, 3) expose a per-tenant flush policy to immediately bypass coalescing. Fastest is to set header at router level for that tenant.

sam.sre: I can flip the router canary to exclude SSE/streaming paths for now. Doing a quick rollback on the proxy_buffering flag for streaming. Rolling back canary for nodes handling /v1/generate?

deploy-bot: canary flag rollback started (router/nginx: fallback-proxy-buffering=false) — ETA 2m.

lee.eng: while rollback proceeds, add a temporary header-based workaround on the tenant route: set X-Accel-Buffering: no and Cache-Control: no-transform. That prevents nginx from coalescing. Marcus can apply to the tenant mapping in Console.

marcus.cs: applied header override for tenant acme-corp. Customer confirmed initial TTFB improves to ~60ms on their next attempts. They reported p99 dropped from ~2.1s -> ~120ms.

julia.support: great, please keep them happy while we root cause fully. Next steps?

taylor.eng: follow-up items: 1) revert the router nginx canary to default (done by @sam.sre), 2) add automated test for streaming endpoints to detect proxy_buffering behavior in canaries, 3) instrument our edge to emit first_chunk_latency and chunk_payload_size metrics per route so we can catch regressions earlier. Also add a canary gating rule that excludes streaming paths from buffer toggles.

sam.sre: have rolled back global canary for streaming-sensitive traffic and flagged the nginx change as the primary cause. Adding a short-term dashboard showing first_chunk p50/p95/p99 per region.

lee.eng: also found code path where continuous batching will delay the first chunk up to flush_after_ms if the request is batched with others. We should ensure small single-request paths bypass the batch window. Filed infra-issue #INF-1298.

marcus.cs: customer is satisfied for now, but asked for a postmortem and a config timeline. I'll handle comms.

julia.support: assign owners: @sam.sre owns rollback verification and canary gating, @lee.eng owns batching bypass patch and tests, @taylor.eng owns metrics and alerting. I'll draft an incident note for CS.

sam.sre: quick note for mitigation checklist we used:
- identify canary toggle correlation (deploy logs + metrics)
- repro locally with small server + nginx to confirm buffering behavior
- apply header override X-Accel-Buffering: no on tenant route
- rollback canary for streaming path in router
- verify customer p99 TTFB returned to baseline

lee.eng: small repro I used (paste):
```python
# tiny server to simulate streaming first chunk
from time import sleep
from flask import Flask, Response
app = Flask(__name__)
@app.route('/')
def s():
    def gen():
        yield 'data: first\n\n'
        sleep(1)
        yield 'data: rest\n\n'
    return Response(gen(), mimetype='text/event-stream')

# curl with and without nginx proxy_buffering to observe TTFB
```

taylor.eng: I'll add an alert rule: if first_chunk_p99 > 500ms for streaming endpoints then page SRE.

marcus.cs: leaving this thread open until postmortem published; customer ok with progress. Thanks all. :thumbsup:

julia.support: noted, will update once postmortem link is available.

deploy-bot: incident-note created: INC-2026-03-14-2271 (links to INF-1298, rollback jobs).
